title: Essentialism, checked against the science

scenes.text: Busy all day, and nothing that matters moved? One best-selling book says you're simply doing too much.

visual.headline: Less, but better. Does it hold up?

scenes.text: In Essentialism, Greg McKeown argues that only a few things are truly vital. So choose them on purpose, and say no to the rest.
His method has three steps. Explore what really matters. Eliminate everything else. Then execute, until the essential becomes routine.
We checked fourteen of the book's claims against the research. Six hold up. Three only partly. Two are contested, and three can't be tested at all.
The practical tools hold up best. In one study, students expected to finish a thesis in about 34 days. They took 55. So yes, build in a buffer.
The weaker parts: its biggest ideas come from the author's own experience, and some of the science it cites has since been revised, or failed to replicate.

visual.headline: Some science has moved on
visual.proof: Learned helplessness revised (2016) · violin practice study not replicated (2019)

scenes.text: Our verdict: worth reading if other people's requests run your calendar. Trust the tools, and treat the big claims as opinion, not science.

visual.headline: Read it for the tools
visual.body: Skip it if you already prioritize strictly

scenes.text: All fourteen claims and their sources are in the description.

audience: Busy professionals and managers deciding whether Essentialism is worth their time (YouTube, LinkedIn)
